extracted.intended_audience: creative writers, especially narrative prose authors
extracted.subtask_description: Craft guidance for making prose ‘sound right’: training the writer’s aural sense, controlling rhythm/pace/forward movement, and using sonic techniques in narrative sentences. Includes exercises to write/read aloud and judge whether sound enhances meaning.

rubrics_metrics.name: The sound of the language / test of a sentence
rubrics_metrics.description: The sound of the language is where it all begins. The test of a sentence is, Does it sound right?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Basic elements of language are physical: noises words make, sounds and silences that make rhythms marking relationships. Both meaning and beauty depend on these sounds and rhythms. This applies equally to prose and poetry (prose sound effects are usually subtle and irregular).

rubrics_metrics.name: Mind’s ear / awareness of your own prose
rubrics_metrics.description: A good writer, like a good reader, has a mind’s ear—an inner ear that hears prose while writing and reading.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Train your mind’s ear to listen to your own prose; cultivate or reawaken oral/aural sensibility so you can hear problems (dull, choppy, droning, jerky, feeble) and strengths (lively, well‑paced, flowing, strong, beautiful).

rubrics_metrics.name: Forward movement: sentence duty to lead on
rubrics_metrics.description: The chief duty of a narrative sentence is to lead to the next sentence—to keep the story going.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Forward movement, pace, and rhythm are central. Pace and movement depend above all on rhythm; the primary way to feel and control rhythm is by hearing it.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid common aural faults / aim for lively qualities
rubrics_metrics.description: Be alert to faults in the sound of prose (dull, choppy, droning, jerky, feeble) and cultivate positive qualities (lively, well‑paced, flowing, strong, beautiful).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These descriptors function as evaluative criteria when judging narrative voice and sentence-level sound.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prose can and should express delight in language
rubrics_metrics.description: A story is made out of language, and language can and does express delight in itself just as music does.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: ‘Being gorgeous’ in prose is legitimate—poetic or striking diction and sound can be used if they serve the prose rather than distract from it.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of sonic techniques (but not rhyme/meter)
rubrics_metrics.description: Use onomatopoeia, alliteration, repetition, rhythmic effects, made‑up words or names, dialect—any kind of sound effect you like—but NOT rhyme or regular meter (this is prose, not poetry).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Write a paragraph-to-page meant to be read aloud; play with sounds and rhythms, show off, and let sound lead you while remembering to avoid poetic meter and rhyme.

rubrics_metrics.name: Read aloud and perform to test and improve prose
rubrics_metrics.description: Read your prose aloud (loudly) and perform it with vigor to hear where the text needs improvement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Performing/listening will almost certainly lead you to improve the text — strengthen sounds, tweak rhythms, and discover voice. If working in a group, performing is fun and the best response to a successful piece is applause.

rubrics_metrics.name: Match sentence rhythm to physical action or emotion
rubrics_metrics.description: Make the rhythm and movement of sentences embody or represent the physical reality or strong emotion you are describing (joy, fear, grief, etc.).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In exercises: describe an action or a person feeling strong emotion and try to have the sentence rhythms embody that feeling or action.

rubrics_metrics.name: Playful, permission‑giving practice (‘Being Gorgeous’ exercise)
rubrics_metrics.description: Write for pleasure and play: relax control, encourage the sounds/beats/echoes to lead you; write noisily or hushed, use dialect, invent words—forgive departures from invisible style while practicing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is not free writing but similar: write for children or ancestors, use any narrating voice, reproduce action in jerky/flowing movement of words, and treat the exercise as a warm‑up to get into the swing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Names and place‑names as sonic devices
rubrics_metrics.description: Names are interesting sounds; the sound of character and place names can be intensively expressive and carry echo‑allusions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider the sound of names (e.g., Uriah Heep, Jane Eyre, Lothlórien, Middle‑earth) as part of your sonic palette when naming characters and settings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sound often conveys meaning — listen beyond expected authors
rubrics_metrics.description: When reading, keep your ear out even with authors you mightn't associate with aural beauty; much meaning may have come through the sound and rhythm of the words.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Study a range of writers (fantasy classics, surprising sources) to notice how sound carries meaning; examples include Kipling, Twain, Hurston, Gloss, Walker, Jewett, Haruf.

rubrics_metrics.name: Evaluate conscious stylistic ornamentation critically
rubrics_metrics.description: When a novelist or essayist visibly strives for striking or poetical prose, ask whether the conscious style does its work as prose.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ask: Do you enjoy it? Does the conscious style intensify what it’s saying or distract you from it? Use this question when judging whether ornate sound choices serve the story.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use short performance/evaluation heuristic: audience reaction
rubrics_metrics.description: For pieces meant to be read aloud, the best response to a successful performance piece is applause; performative success is a useful heuristic of effectiveness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In group settings, not much critiquing may be required—listen for audience reaction as an indicator of whether the sound and delivery worked.
